title: The Trust and Safety Vendor Evaluation Checklist for Mid-Market Teams
summary: An eight-area checklist, a scoring table, and a shadow-mode trial plan for mid-market trust and safety teams evaluating a moderation vendor.
body_markdown:
Mid-market trust and safety teams usually buy once and live with the choice for years. The platform sits inside your review queues, your enforcement decisions, and your reporting to leadership and regulators. A demo with clean sample data tells you very little about how it will behave on your content.


Use this checklist to structure the evaluation before you take the first vendor call.


## **Before you start: define what you are buying**


Write down three things first.


• The harms in scope. List the abuse types you need to catch, such as harassment, fraud, child safety, adult content, spam, and scams. Rank them by volume and by severity.


• The decisions you make today. Map the actions your team takes: remove, restrict, escalate, warn, ban, or allow. Note who makes each call and how long it takes.


• The numbers you want to move. Pick two or three measures, such as review backlog, time to action, reviewer agreement, appeal overturn rate, or cost per decision. If you do not measure these today, start a baseline now.


## **The checklist**


### **1. Detection quality on your content**


Ask each vendor to run against a labeled sample from your own platform, including your hardest edge cases. Public benchmarks are a useful baseline, and your own sample shows how the system handles your users, your languages, and your slang.


• Request precision and recall for each harm type, not a single blended accuracy number.


• Test at more than one threshold so you can see the tradeoff between missed harm and over-enforcement.


• Include content in every format you host: text, images, video, audio, and profiles.


• Ask how the system performs on new abuse patterns it has not seen before.


### **2. Policy alignment**


• Can you encode your own policy language and thresholds?


• When your policy changes, how quickly can the system reflect it, and how do you verify the change?


• Does the vendor show you why a decision was made, in terms your reviewers recognize?


### **3. Human review operations**


Most mid-market teams still rely on human reviewers for the hardest decisions. The tooling around them matters as much as the model.


• Review queues that can be routed by harm type, severity, and reviewer skill.


• Reviewer context: the content, the user's history, and the policy that applies.


• Support for managed review services if you need to scale without hiring.


### **4. QA and ground truth**


Ask how you will know the system stays accurate after launch.


• Golden sets built from your own reviewed decisions.


• Sampling and double review for quality checks.


• Reviewer agreement tracking and a process to resolve disagreements.


• A way to feed corrected decisions back into the system.


### **5. Escalation paths**


Some cases should never be handled automatically. Confirm the vendor supports clear escalation for high-severity harms, legal requests, and ambiguous cases, with named owners and response targets.


### **6. Audit and reporting**


• A complete record of each decision: the input, the action, the policy applied, and who or what made the call.


• Exports that support regulatory reporting and internal reviews.


• Appeals and case management that link back to the original decision.


### **7. Integration with your existing stack**


• API coverage for your content types and volumes.


• Fit with your current case management, data warehouse, and moderation tools.


• A realistic implementation plan with owners, timelines, and what your engineers need to build.


### **8. Data protection and legal review**


Bring legal and data protection reviewers in early. They often set the pace of the whole deal.


• Where data is stored and processed, and for how long.


• Whether your content is used to train models, and under what terms.


• Subprocessors, security certifications, and incident response commitments.


• A sandboxed environment where you can test with limited data before any production commitment.


## **A simple scoring table**


Score each vendor from 1 to 5 on every row, then weight the rows by what matters most to your team.


Area Question to answer Weight (your call) Score (1 to 5)


Detection quality Does it perform on our labeled sample, by harm type?


Policy alignment Does it follow our policies and thresholds?


Human review Do our reviewers get the context and routing they need?


QA and ground truth Can we measure accuracy and improve it over time?


Escalation Are high-severity cases routed to the right owner?


Audit and reporting Can we reconstruct and defend any decision?


Integration Does it fit our stack within our timeline?


Data protection Does it clear legal and security review?


## **Run the trial in shadow mode**


The strongest evidence comes from running a vendor on live traffic without letting it act. In a shadow-mode trial, the vendor reviews the same content as your current process, and you compare the results side by side.


• Pick a bounded slice of your queue, such as one harm type or one content format.


• Run the vendor in parallel with your incumbent process for a fixed period.


• Compare decisions against your golden set and your reviewers' final calls.


• Measure accuracy, turnaround time, and the cases where the two disagree.


• Review those disagreements with your policy team and decide who was right and why.


• Cut over only after the results meet the targets you set before the trial began.


This approach lowers switching risk, because you validate accuracy and turnaround before any production change.


## Common questions


### How long should a trust and safety vendor evaluation take?


Plan for several weeks. Allow time for scoping, legal and security review, a sandboxed proof, and a shadow-mode trial. Starting legal review at the beginning keeps the timeline from stalling at the end.


### What should we ask for in a vendor demo?


Ask the vendor to run on your own labeled data, show the decision record for individual cases, and demonstrate how a policy change is applied and verified.


### Should we build our own tooling instead?


Building makes sense when you have engineering capacity, stable policies, and a narrow harm scope. Many mid-market teams find that maintaining detection, review tooling, QA, and reporting together costs more than expected. Score your internal option against the same checklist so the comparison is fair.


### Who should be in the evaluation?


Trust and safety, policy, operations, engineering, and legal or data protection. Give each group a section of the checklist to own.


### What does a good vendor relationship look like after launch?


Regular QA reviews, a clear process for updating policies, and shared reporting on the measures you set at the start.
